discovery: Optical lattice clocks and precision timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics; precision measurement and optical metrology
motivation: Hidetoshi Katori conceived the optical lattice clock, trapping thousands of neutral atoms in a 'magic-wavelength' optical lattice so that the light shift of the clock transition cancels. This broke with the belief that trapped-atom clocks must suffer perturbations, combining the Lamb-Dicke confinement of ions with the statistical power of many atoms. Jun Ye turned the concept into the most precise measuring instruments ever made, reaching fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and below, resolving gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample, and pioneering spin-squeezed and many-body-limited clock operation. Built on the frequency-comb revolution, these clocks now drive the redefinition of the SI second, enable relativistic geodesy, and provide sensitive tests of fundamental physics, including searches for dark matter and variations of fundamental constants. Their work exemplifies how quantum control of matter and light yields measurement capabilities of profound scientific and technological consequence.
